Layer 1 · Acquisition Engine · Assessment & Reference

Mallory Layer-1 Crawler

A defence-intelligence acquisition crawler running as a 12-instance fleet on a 40-core box. This document rates it against what a production crawler is expected to do, and documents how it actually works — the architecture, the fetch ladder, the control plane, and the reasoning behind the choices that look unusual.

The rating, first

A working production system with an immature operational layer

The honest summary: the crawler is production-grade; the operation around it is not yet. Weighted across twelve dimensions the system scores 3.4 / 5 — which in practice means it does the hard part well and the boring part badly.

The hard part is genuinely hard and genuinely done. A four-tier fetch ladder that clears Cloudflare-interactive challenges by calling out to a real GPU. A durable per-job frontier that survives restarts. Content-hash dedup with a deliberate bias toward re-fetching. Multilingual keyword gating that does not quietly discard non-English sites. 1.22 million documents from 719 sources in three weeks is not a prototype's output.

The boring part is where the daily bug-fixing comes from. There is no CI. Deployment is a hand-run script. The application log was being discarded entirely until two days ago. Watchdogs exist but have been observed declining to act for eleven hours while narrating that they were declining. Almost every incident of the last three weeks has been the same shape — a component that was working, stopped, and nothing said so — and that is an observability and automation deficit, not a crawler deficit.

What the bug rate actually indicates

114 commits in 27 days with near-daily fixes reads like instability, but the distribution matters. Very few of those commits fixed a crawl-logic error. The large majority fixed silent failures: a capped watcher that resumed nothing, a stop flag that outlived its teardown, a cleanup that abandoned live processes, a log that never reached stdout. That is the signature of a system whose functionality outran its instrumentation — normal for three weeks old, and it is converging: the invariant checks added along the way now catch this class before an operator does.

Measured against production-crawler expectations

Scorecard

Twelve dimensions, each scored 0–5 against what a crawler operating at this scale is expected to provide. Evidence is from the running system, not from intent.

DimensionScoreEvidenceGap
Fetch capability 4.5 Four-tier ladder C1→C4. Measured live mix: 1,212,126 pages via C1 httpx, 6,697 via CamoFox stealth render, 427 via the host GPU solver. Clears Cloudflare-interactive and Incapsula; image captchas solved locally by a vision model. C4 depends on one workstation over an SSH tunnel.
Politeness & compliance 4.5 robots.txt honoured with a deliberate asymmetry: absent robots fails open, but unreadable robots fails closed for .gov/.mil. Per-host concurrency limiter. Compliance audit rows written for careful hosts only. Host blocklist applied at both enqueue and seed. —
Data quality 4.0 Content-hash dedup, 9.4% duplicate rate across 1.22M rows. Conditional GETs via ETag/Last-Modified. Multilingual: English is 68%, with French, Spanish, German, Italian, Turkish and Portuguese all material. Extraction quality is deliberately deferred to Layer 2.
Durability & resume 4.0 Per-job frontier in SQLite: pending URLs, the seen set, and spent page budget all restored, so a resumed job cannot overshoot max_pages or re-walk the site. Frontiers are container-local; moving one needs a dedicated tool.
Testing 4.0 1,337 test functions in 140 files, 24k lines — a 0.73 test-to-code ratio. Tests routinely encode the measured incident that motivated them, so regressions name their own history. No CI runs them. Some share the production database.
Cost control 4.0 Paid proxy egress has exactly one owner instance, because the spend counter is a read-modify-write file and N writers would silently defeat the daily cap. No per-job cost attribution.
Scheduling & coverage 3.5 Adaptive cadence driven by measured changes-per-day. Sitemap cross-check treats an exhausted frontier as distinct from a covered site. 94.7% of catalogued sources have pages. 672 of 760 sites are still in the initial probe phase; only 12 have reached steady cadence.
Security & isolation 3.5 SSRF guard, per-host TLS proceed-anyway that is off by default and only after a real cert failure, cpuset isolation between workloads, dashboards bound to localhost behind a tunnel. Dashboard password+OTP is built and tested but disarmed for want of a mail relay.
Observability 3.0 Per-site drill-down dashboards, an unresolved-page issues log with a cause taxonomy, and six live invariants asserted against production state rather than mocks. The orchestrator's entire application log was silently dropped until 15 Aug. No metrics store; no alerting.
Resilience 3.0 Three distinct host circuit breakers, wall-clock deflection budget, autopilot pressing health actions on a timer, engine-level RAM and CPU governors that read their own cgroup. Watchdogs observed declining to act. CamoFox was down 11 hours with its watchdog logging the fact 660 times.
Scale & throughput 3.0 ~61k pages/day sustained over 20 days. Horizontal scaling by domain-sharded instances is proven at 12. Render-bound at roughly 2.5 pages/s on a GPU-less box; ~1.2 cores per concurrent render is the ceiling.
Deployment & ops 2.5 Reproducible image build; one image shared by all 12 instances so the fleet cannot run mixed code. No CI/CD. Deploys are hand-run rolling scripts. Five compose files. Code reaches the box by scp, not by a tracked revision.

How to read the weighting

The three lowest scores — deployment, resilience, observability — are the three that produce the daily bug-fixing. They are also the cheapest to lift, because none of them require new crawler capability. Adding CI alone would move deployment from 2.5 to 4 and would have caught at least two of this week's regressions before they reached the fleet.

Scope

What the crawler is for

Mallory Layer 1 is an acquisition engine. Its job ends at "we have the page, it is relevant, here is its text and its raw HTML". It deliberately does not interpret. Classification into tenders, partnerships, competitive signals and company events is Layer 2's work, operating on the raw text and the flat tags Layer 1 hands over.

That boundary is load-bearing. It is why the keep-gate is a mechanical keyword match and not a judgement, why the deduplicator refuses to merge different URLs about the same event, and why the document model carries detection tags as informational fields rather than typed records.

What it does

  • Crawls a catalogue of ~760 defence-industry manufacturer and trade-press sites on an adaptive cadence.
  • Escalates through four fetch tiers when a site resists, including clearing interactive Cloudflare challenges.
  • Filters every page against a global multilingual keyword corpus before storing it.
  • Deduplicates against its own history, and issues conditional GETs so an unchanged page costs almost nothing.
  • Stores structured documents in Postgres and PDF blobs in MinIO.
  • Registers accounts and maintains logged-in sessions where a portal gates its data.
  • Tracks coverage per site, and can fetch pages a site publishes but never links to.

System shape

Architecture

Four services, one shared data plane, and a control plane that is the only thing allowed to talk to the fleet.

Why the control plane is separate

The crawler knows how to crawl a job. It does not know which sites exist, when they were last visited, or whether a site is worth visiting again. Keeping that knowledge in a separate service means the crawler stays a stateless-ish worker that can be restarted, scaled and sharded without losing the catalogue — and it means every dashboard panel reads one orchestrator endpoint, so fanning out across twelve instances required no dashboard changes at all.

Data stores and what each one owns

StoreOwnsWhy here
Postgres documentsThe corpus — text, HTML, metadataLayer 2 reads it directly; needs relational provenance queries
MinIOPDF blobs onlyBlobs are shared across duplicate rows, so they must not be row-scoped
crawl_history.sqliteFrontier, seen set, budgets, dedup validatorsPer instance — it is the resume point, and it must be local to the engine that owns it
orchestrator.dbSource catalogue, schedules, coverage ledger, shard mapSurvives fleet restarts; it is the system's memory of intent

Fetch strategy

The four-tier ladder

Most pages are cheap. A few are guarded. Spending browser time on the cheap ones is how a crawler becomes slow, so the engine starts at the cheapest possible fetch and escalates only when the page refuses.

the ladder ends at a workstation instead of a container

Cloudflare's interactive tier never self-clears inside Docker, and the decisive difference is the graphics stack, not the engine and not the IP. In a container Chrome reports ANGLE (Mesa, llvmpipe); on the workstation it reports a real GPU and passes. That capability surface is cross-checked in JavaScript and cannot be faked away. The data centre has no GPU either — measured, not assumed — so C4 calls out over an SSH tunnel to the only real GPU in the system.

a cleared session is reused rather than re-solved

The clearance cookie is bound to the TLS and HTTP/2 fingerprint of the browser that earned it, so it does not transplant to another engine — but it keeps working in the same session. The first URL on a guarded host pays ~10 s; every subsequent URL is an ordinary fast navigation. Without that reuse a 50-page guarded site would cost 50 × 28 s.

success is judged on content, never on status

The characteristic failure of every tier is a 200 OK that is still the interstitial. Any check that trusts the status code calls that a success. Each tier therefore inspects the returned title and body for challenge markers before accepting the page.

Per-page path

What happens to one page

A number that looks alarming and is not

A 30% keep rate reads like a broken filter until you see the split: ~42% dropped by the keyword gate and ~22% skipped as unchanged. The gate rejecting most of a general-purpose news site is the gate working. The figure to watch is not the keep rate but whether the drops are multilingual — an English-only gate once condemned around 40 non-English portals, which is why the corpus now matches folded substring stems across languages.

the gate fails open on an empty corpus

If the keyword file is missing or unreadable, the gate keeps everything rather than dropping everything. A misconfigured filter that silently zeroes the output is far more damaging than one that temporarily over-collects, and it is much harder to notice.

every dedup uncertainty resolves to "changed"

A false "changed" wastes one re-crawl. A false "unchanged" loses data permanently. The classifier is deliberately asymmetric in favour of the cheap mistake.

Horizontal scale

The fleet, and why it is shaped this way

Twelve containers, one engine process each, pinned to cores 0–19, each owning a disjoint set of domains.

processes, not more workers in one process

A page costs about 0.4 CPU-core-seconds and 97% of that is Python, so one CPython process tops out around 1.5–3 cores regardless of how many tabs it owns. The engine has a multiprocess mode and it must stay at 1: its children share no memory with the API parent, so the dashboard reads zero for the whole crawl, a child booting after STOP deletes the shared stop file and its siblings carry on, the paid-proxy spend cap is defeated, and resume breaks outright. Every one of those is parent/child divergence inside one container. A container running exactly one engine has none of them. Measured at two instances: 9.26 pages/s combined against 3.90 for one.

a domain is assigned once and never reassigned

A site's frontier — its pending URLs, its seen set, its spent budget — lives inside one container's SQLite. Route it elsewhere and the crawl silently restarts from the seed while the real progress sits unreachable next door. Hashing alone is only stable while the instance count is: adding one instance moves most domains under % N, and the frontiers do not move with them. So the first sighting of a domain fixes its instance permanently, which makes growth free and shrinking a deliberate operation.

blake2b, never Python's hash()

PYTHONHASHSEED is randomised per process, so hash("example.com") % 12 gives a different answer after every restart — which would re-shard the entire fleet on each deploy.

cpusets, not CPU quotas

Under a hard CFS quota the scheduler throttles the container, latency inflates, the per-item watchdog fires, and weak-host demotion drops those hosts to concurrency 1 — so a CPU cap makes throughput collapse below baseline instead of levelling off. A cpuset gives hard separation with full speed inside the set. The box is divided crawler 0–19, L2 processing 20–29, SFL 30–34, shared and OS 35–39.

A trap this cost real time

Both the RAM brake and the CPU governor originally read the host's figures, so neither could see the cgroup it was actually confined by. The RAM brake never fired at any container limit — a 20 GiB cap nearly OOM-killed three instances — and the CPU governor throttled on host-wide load caused by neighbours. Any governor inside a container must read memory.max/memory.current and its own cpuset, never /proc/meminfo.

Layer 1.5

The control plane

The orchestrator decides what to crawl and when; the fleet decides only how.

Adaptive cadence

Each site moves through three phases: baseline (never crawled — one census crawl that measures existence, not change), probe (crawled at least once, cadence is a category guess clamped to at most weekly while real signal accumulates), and steady (two or more measurements and ten days of history, so cadence is chosen from a measured change rate).

the change rate is per day, not per run

This is the single most important decision in the scheduler. A per-run rate is self-reinforcing: put a site on monthly and each crawl finds a month of accumulated changes, so it always looks very active and ratchets back to daily; put it on daily and each crawl finds almost nothing, so it decays to monthly. Only a time-normalised rate is invariant to the cadence you happen to be running.

nothing bootstraps straight to monthly

A wrong monthly guess means sixty days blind before the second data point. Measure fast, settle slow.

Live invariants

Six checks assert against the running system rather than against mocks, because every fault in this project's history passed its unit tests. They were not logic bugs in a function — they were a working system quietly doing nothing.

InvariantCatches
write pathIngest returning 200 while the row never reaches Postgres
tiers reachedA fetch tier that is configured but never actually exercised
c4 uniform + reachableA partly-configured fleet, where whether a guarded site is fetched depends on which shard owns it
dispatch routingWork being sent to an instance that does not hold its frontier
no wedged instancerunning=true with an empty queue and an idle CPU — a teardown that never finished
seed copies agreeInstances silently running different seed data
Design note

The C4 invariant deliberately does not solve a real URL — that would drive a browser through a third-party challenge every 15 minutes. It asserts liveness plus identity, because the solver's health endpoint returns fields no other service would return, and it says so in its own detail text rather than implying it proved more than it did.

errors.py is worth singling out: it is pure classification and policy tables that import nothing from the rest of the package. That is what lets the fetcher, the engine and the harvester all agree on what a failure means without a circular dependency — and it is why a mis-bucketed reason once had fleet-wide consequences, when host_busy defaulted to "terminal" and buried 617 recoverable URLs.

Roads not taken

Decisions that look strange until you know why

one event loop and one thread, instead of locks

Every Playwright object lives on a single loop; only plain data crosses to a worker thread. Because cooperative scheduling makes any section without an await atomic, shared mutable state — the frontier, per-job counters, the crawl history — needs almost no locking. The cost is discipline: touching Playwright from another thread is a class of bug that cannot occur, but touching shared state around an await is one that can, and did (a drain race once cancelled workers with items still in flight).

depth is minimum hops, not descent order

With a LIFO frontier and first-sight-final depth, one site recorded depth 1,826 for articles three hops from the seed. Depth is now relaxed toward the minimum whenever a shorter path is discovered, which is what makes depth limits mean what an operator thinks they mean.

pagination links are front-loaded and action links are dropped

On a rate-limited listing, roughly half of a page's links can be vote/login/redirect controls. Following them burns the request budget the real pages need, and the crawler ends up storing the navigation bar instead of the content. Pagination is prioritised; action links are skipped.

the sitemap is a check, not a seed

Seeding from a sitemap makes coverage look complete by construction. Used as a cross-check instead, it answers the question that matters: the site publishes N URLs, we have M — and an exhausted frontier is not the same thing as a covered site.

a bounded cleanup now kills what it abandons

Teardown gives every close 5 seconds and moves on, because a wedged browser close never returns and waiting on one once left a batch stuck at running=true forever. But the abandonment was justified with "the process is ending and the init reaper handles the children" — and neither half held: teardown runs at the end of every batch with the container staying up, and an init reaper collects zombies while a browser that ignored close() is very much alive. Each timed-out teardown orphaned a whole driver tree. Measured: one instance holding 24 browsers under twelve separate drivers where a healthy one holds 2 under one.

Pattern recognition

The failure classes that keep recurring

Three weeks of incidents cluster into a small number of shapes. Naming them is what turned the fixes from whack-a-mole into a checklist.

ClassSignatureSeen as
Silent success An operation reports OK and changes nothing "Dispatched 1,457 URLs" that dispatched none; a resume the crawler refused without raising; ingest returning 200 while the row never landed
Silent nothing A watcher that cannot act, and does not say so Auto-refill capped below the busy count, resuming nothing for days while the fleet drained 12 → 9 → 7
Unreachable power A capability shipped, correct, and never invoked Real-Chrome impersonation gated behind status in (401, 403), when a TLS refusal has no status at all
Abandoned cleanup Giving up on a close, and calling that reaping 2,266 leaked browser processes fleet-wide against a ~300 baseline
Blind governor A limiter measuring the wrong scope RAM and CPU brakes reading host figures from inside a cgroup
Fan-out that didn't A fleet operation that quietly hit instance 0 only 485 of 507 scheduled re-crawls had never run; flush leaving 11 of 12 histories intact
Invisible log The diagnostic exists and is discarded No basicConfig, so every log.info in the orchestrator fell to the last-resort handler and was dropped
The uncomfortable part

The invariant checker written specifically to catch these classes committed two of them itself within an hour of going live — one probe treated as a verdict, and a count that quietly redefined "all" as "all the ones that answered". The lesson is not that the checks are useless; it is that "assert against production" is a discipline that has to be applied to the checker too.

The honest list

What is still missing

Would materially reduce the daily fixing

  1. Continuous integration. 1,337 tests exist and nothing runs them automatically. Two regressions this week reached the fleet and would not have. This is the single highest-value gap.
  2. A tracked deploy path. Code reaches the box by scp; the box is not a checkout of anything. There is no way to answer "which revision is instance 7 running?" without inspecting the container.
  3. Alerting. Every incident so far was found by a person looking. The invariants exist and produce verdicts; nothing carries a failing verdict to a human.
  4. Watchdogs that act. At least two watchdogs currently detect and narrate rather than remediate.

Known operational debt

  • Dashboard authentication is built and tested but disarmed, pending a mail relay credential.
  • Tests share the production database, so real crawl state can fail a suite in ways that look like engine bugs.
  • 672 of 760 sites remain in the initial probe phase; the adaptive cadence has not yet had enough history to settle most of the catalogue.
  • Five jobs hold frontier rows with no saved config and can never be resumed.
  • C4 depends on a single workstation and an SSH tunnel; there is no second GPU anywhere in the system.
  • Five compose files, with two of them keying on a literal service name — siblings silently lose their limits and tunnel dependency.

Not gaps, despite appearances

  • The 30% keep rate. The gate is doing its job; the split is 42% gated and 22% unchanged.
  • The ~2.5 pages/s ceiling. That is roughly 1.2 cores per concurrent render on a GPU-less box. It is a hardware fact, not a tuning failure — more workers cannot beat it.
  • Layer 1 not classifying anything. Deliberate. Interpretation is Layer 2's contract.
Where this sits

Three weeks in, with 1.22 million documents from 719 sources and a fetch stack that clears defences most commercial crawlers do not attempt, the acquisition capability is ahead of where a three-week-old system usually is. The operational envelope around it is behind. That asymmetry is the whole finding — and it is the reason the fix list above is short, cheap and mostly not about crawling.
